query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: A hybrid machine learning model, trained on a limited set of high-throughput first-principles and select in‐situ thermodynamic measurements, can accurately and efficiently predict the melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties for high-entropy alloys over a wide range of compositions, achieving prediction errors similar to traditional DSC/CALPHAD methods.
generation.material_initial_state: Solid-state high-entropy alloys near the solid-to-liquid transition.
generation.intervention: Application of a hybrid ML approach that integrates curated high-throughput thermodynamic data from first-principles calculations and targeted in-situ melting experiments.
generation.conditions: High-temperature regimes near the melting point across a broad compositional space of multi-principal element alloys.
generation.structural_mediator: A surrogate model (e.g., deep neural network or ensemble regression) that learns complex correlations between elemental descriptors and thermodynamic outputs, effectively mediating between input composition and melting behavior.
generation.mechanism: The model leverages available high-fidelity thermodynamic data to capture the influential multi-element interactions and structural factors that govern phase transitions. By combining first-principles insights with in-situ measured properties, it generates predictive correlations that replicate detailed DSC and CALPHAD results, yet at a fraction of the time and cost.
generation.predicted_outcome: The model will predict melting temperatures, fusion enthalpy/entropy, and volume changes at melting with errors typically within ±5–10% compared to traditional methods, and will deliver rapid predictions over the entire HEA compositional space.
generation.baseline: Traditional methods such as differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), differential thermal analysis (DTA), and full-scale CALPHAD assessments for each individual alloy composition.
generation.boundary: The model's accuracy may be limited in compositional regions with very sparse training data or where novel synergistic elemental effects occur; also, kinetic effects near melting are not directly captured by equilibrium-based data.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainty exists regarding the predictive performance in novel elemental combinations not well represented in the training set, and the potential for overfitting to targeted high-fidelity inputs. Moreover, the model may inadequately capture transient, non-equilibrium phenomena during melting.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a set of 10–15 high-entropy alloy compositions that were not used for training the ML model. Synthesize these alloys and perform standardized DSC measurements, high-temperature neutron imaging, and calorimetric experiments to determine the melting temperature, enthalpy of fusion, entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and select liquid-phase thermodynamic properties. Compare these experimental values with the surrogate model predictions.
measurements: Fusion enthalpy and entropy via calorimetry
Volume change at melting from in-situ imaging
Liquid-phase thermodynamic properties from high-temperature experiments
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If more than 30% of the tested compositions show prediction errors exceeding ±10% relative to the experimental measurements for the key thermodynamic parameters, then the hybrid ML approach is falsified as an accurate and efficient methodology for determining these properties across the HEA family.

AbstractThe ability to predict and understand phases in high-entropy alloys (HEAs) is still being debated, and primarily true predictive capabilities derive from the known thermodynamics of materials. The present work demonstrates that prior work using high-throughput first-principles calculations may be further utilized to provide direct insight into the temperature- and composition-dependent phase evolution in HEAs, particularly Al-containing HEAs with a strengthening multiphase microstructure. Using a simple model with parameters derived from first-principles calculations, we reproduce the major features associated with Al-containing phases, demonstrating a generalizable approach for exploring potential phase evolution where little experimental data exists. Neutron scattering, in situ microscopy, and calorimetry measurements suggest that our high-throughput Monte Carlo technique captures both qualitative and quantitative features for both intermetallic phase formation and microstructure evolution at lower temperatures. This study provides a simple approach to guide HEA development, including ordered multi-phase HEAs, which may prove valuable for structural applications. Explorat

In recent years, several groups have devised computational strategies to identify and characterize HE alloys. For example, Troparevsky et al. used “high-throughput” density-functional theory calculations of formation energies to predict which combination of elements is likely to form an HE alloy. In addition, Senkov et al. employed a calculated phase diagram (CALPHAD)-based combinatorial approach to screen computationally a large number of candidate metal alloys for those forming only solid–solution phases. Beyond these studies, other workers have formulated predictive metrics, such as average melting temperature and average valence electron concentration, to characterize relatively simple correlations between the metrics and the propensity to form HE alloys. Most recently, Sarker et al. proposed using a new descriptor, the entropy-forming ability, to predict HE alloys having high hardnesses and validated its use by combining first-principles and experimental synthesis. AbstractThe third-generation thermodynamic descriptions for Ta-Cr and Ta-V binary systems were performed to construct the reliable thermodynamic database for refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) containing Laves phase. The third-generation Gibbs energy expressions of pure Cr and V in both solid and liquid phases were established, from which the thermodynamic properties and thermal vacancy can be well described. The thermodynamic descriptions of Ta-Cr and Ta-V over the whole composition and temperature regions were carried out based on the reviewed phase equilibria and thermodynamic data with the CALPHAD (CALculation of PHAse Diagrams) approach. Specifically, the thermodynamic parameters of C14 and C15 Laves phases were evaluated by combining the theoretically computed and experimentally measured thermodynamic properties as well as the semiempirical relations. The calculated phase diagrams and thermodynamic properties in Ta-Cr and Ta-V systems according to the present thermodynamic parameters had a nice agreement with the experimental data even down to 0 K, indicating the reliability of the present modeling.Keywords: third-generation thermodynamic description, Ta-Cr system, Ta-V s

decision.trend: Early work (PMC4366518) combined simple rules with high-throughput phase diagram calculations to screen vast multi-principal alloy spaces. Subsequent studies (PMC6207727) refined predictive thermodynamic modeling of HEA phase evolution using first-principles approaches. Real-time neutron imaging (PMC8320920) then enabled direct observation of melting processes and liquid-state behavior, but the method remains relatively resource-intensive. More recently, data-driven models (PMC6565683) tackled broader composition spaces by learning from limited data, but still rely on high-quality, consistent thermodynamic inputs. A robust approach to systematically measure and predict melting temperature, fusion enthalpy/entropy, and volume changes across the enormous HEA design space, with validated accuracy and low cost, has yet to be fully realized.
decision.unsolved: No single method yet provides rapid, high-fidelity coverage of all key thermodynamic properties at scale. Existing approaches—high-throughput phase diagram calculations, specialized in-situ measurements, and data-driven modeling—each address different aspects but lack a fully integrated, validated procedure for robustly determining melting, fusion, and liquid-phase properties over the wide range of multi-principal chemistries.
decision.lever: A hybrid ML approach incorporating targeted high-throughput thermodynamic data (e.g., from first-principles and selected in-situ experiments) to train property-surrogate models for melting and liquid-phase parameters across wide HEA composition ranges
decision.why: Combining curated thermodynamic data, in-situ measurements of melting, and established computational results within a machine-learning framework can scale efficiently to the combinatorial space of HEAs. Such a model can deliver accurate predictions for key metrics—melting points, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume changes—while providing a robust, experimentally and computationally validated approach that can be decisively ruled out if its surrogate predictions fail when benchmarked against a well-chosen set of measured complex compositions.
